§06-001 Axios cross-runtime features

2 Lessons 00m00s / 00m00s
The concept Your first request One configured client: `axios.create` Typing requests Narrowing errors Running requests in parallel
Build Modern Web Apps with React, Hooks, State Management, and APIs Using Vite or Next.js Running your first React project
08m10s

In-depth walkthrough of Axios cross-runtime features, examining real-world production implementations, rendering performance, and TypeScript contracts.

Official Documentation References
Axios Official Documentation — Promise-based HTTP client for the browser and node.js.
Axios: Interceptors Reference — Intercepting requests and responses before handling.
📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

A travel adapter is a small block with one socket on the front and a different plug on the back. Your laptop charger never learns about British, European, or Japanese outlets. It plugs into the same socket every time, and the block deals with the wall. Axios is that block for HTTP. Your code calls `axios.get(...)` and gets a promise back. Underneath, the library picks the plug that fits the runtime it woke up in: `XMLHttpRequest` in a browser, Node's `http` module on a server, or `fetch` when you ask for it.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

The moment your app runs in two places, this stops being a style question. A component fetches in the browser; the same endpoint gets called during server rendering, in a route handler, or in a test. One client with one response shape means one set of error paths to reason about instead of a browser branch and a server branch. The pieces here are also the substrate for the rest of this section. TanStack Query needs a query function that returns a promise and honors an `AbortSignal`; a wrapped Axios call is exactly that. React's cleanup story for in-flight requests is `AbortController`. The single-client pattern from `axios.create` is where interceptors, auth headers, and XSRF configuration eventually live.

Key Code / CLI Example
// Three ways to consume the same promise.
axios.get("/api/users").then((response) => console.log(response.data));

const response = await axios.get("/api/users"); // inside an async function

axios
  .get("/api/users")
  .then((response) => console.log(response.data))
  .catch((error) => console.error(error.message))
  .finally(() => console.log("done"));
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

**Reading fields off the response instead of `data`.** The `fetch` habit of `response.json()` and `response.ok` does not carry over. Axios has already parsed the body. There is no second step to await. Axios already ran the response transform and parsed the body before the promise settled. The same error shape hits `response.ok`: Fix: `const post = response.data;` and check `response.status` when you need the code. **Touching a caught error before narrowing it.**

§06-002 HTTP with Axios

2 Lessons 00m00s / 00m00s
A waiter who handles the entire call The smallest useful request Method aliases Request configuration Cancellation with AbortController Errors you can branch on
React: Creating and Hosting a Full-Stack Site Making requests with auth tokens
07m07s

In-depth walkthrough of HTTP with Axios, examining real-world production implementations, rendering performance, and TypeScript contracts.

Official Documentation References
Axios Official Documentation — Promise-based HTTP client for the browser and node.js.
Axios: Interceptors Reference — Intercepting requests and responses before handling.
📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

Imagine calling a restaurant. With the browser's built-in `fetch`, you get a phone, dial the restaurant, listen for an answer, and decide for yourself whether a busy signal counts as an error. You also have to hand-parse the JSON and unwrap the response yourself. Axios is the full-service equivalent: it dials, listens, decides what counts as a failure, parses the body for you, and hands back a tidy `{ data, status, statusText, headers, config, request }` object. The previous chapter showed you what axios *is* (Promise-based, isomorphic, same API in Node and the browser). This chapter shows you what axios *does* for you on every call: method aliases that match HTTP verbs, a request-config object that consolidates everything you'd otherwise spell out, structured errors with codes you can branch on, query-parameter serialization that you can override, headers as a case-insensitive map, cancellation through the standard `AbortController`, and instance defaults so a `baseURL` is not repeated across a thousand call sites.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Every feature chapter after this one assumes you can talk to an HTTP API. Axios is the most-used HTTP client in the React ecosystem precisely because the response shape is consistent, the errors are structured, and the cancellation works with the same `AbortController` you already use in `useEffect`. The config object (`baseURL`, `timeout`, `signal`, `validateStatus`, `redact`) replaces half a dozen ad-hoc wrappers that you'd otherwise build per project. Method aliases match the verbs in your API spec; `postForm` matches the `multipart/form-data` shape you actually send when uploading; `getUri` matches the URL you'd build when you want to share it. The structured `AxiosError` is what lets the chapter on TanStack Query decide, on a per-request basis, whether to retry, redirect, or surface a message. Without `isAxiosError`, without `error.response`, without `error.code`, that decision is guesswork.

Key Code / CLI Example
import axios from "axios";

const response = await axios.get("https://api.example.com/posts/1");
console.log(response.data); // already parsed as JSON
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

**Forgetting `await` on a request.** `axios.get(...)` returns a `Promise<AxiosResponse<T>>`, not the response. Logging `axios.get("/x")` prints a promise object. `await` it, or `.then((r) => ...)` it. **Reading `response` instead of `response.data`.** The HTTP status and headers live on `response`; the parsed body lives on `response.data`. `console.log(response)` dumps the wrapper, not your data. **Forgetting to set a `timeout`.** Without one, a stalled request hangs forever. The promise never resolves and your loading spinner spins until the user navigates away. Always pass `timeout` on production requests: **Treating `fetch`'s "no HTTP error" behavior as Axios's.** With `fetch`, a `404` resolves and you have to check `response.ok` yourself. With axios, a `4xx`/`5xx` rejects by default

§06-003 Capture upload and download progress

2 Lessons 00m00s / 00m00s
A scale under the conveyor belt The two callbacks Minimal example: an upload bar Predict the render Common mistakes Where the rest of the config lives
Build Modern Web Apps with React, Hooks, State Management, and APIs Using Vite or Next.js Understanding props
01m45s

In-depth walkthrough of Capture upload and download progress, examining real-world production implementations, rendering performance, and TypeScript contracts.

Official Documentation References
TanStack React Query Documentation — Powerful asynchronous state management, server-state caching, and query hooks.
TanStack Query: Important Defaults & Invalidation — Stale-while-revalidate caching, garbage collection, and query client invalidation.
📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

A shipping company loads a truck through a conveyor belt with a scale under it. The scale does not report every gram as it passes. It shouts out a running total three times a second: "40 kilos loaded, moving at 12 kilos per second, about 7 seconds left." That is enough for the loading-dock display, and it keeps the person reading the display from going cross-eyed. Axios does the same thing with bytes. You hand it a callback, and while the request body goes out (or the response body comes in) axios calls that callback with how much has moved so far, how fast, and how much is left. Like the scale, it deliberately throttles itself: at most three calls per second.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Anything that moves more than a few kilobytes needs a progress signal, or the user assumes the app is broken and clicks the button again. Duplicate uploads created by an impatient second click are a real class of bug, and a progress bar plus a disabled button is the whole fix. The download side matters for a different reason: `total` being `undefined` is normal, not exceptional. A server behind gzip or a streaming endpoint gives you `loaded` and nothing else. Code written on the assumption that `progress` is always a number renders `NaN%` in production while looking fine in dev against a local file server. The optional types on `AxiosProgressEvent` are the type checker telling you about that in advance.

Key Code / CLI Example
import { useState } from "react";
import axios, { type AxiosProgressEvent } from "axios";

export function AvatarUpload(): React.ReactElement {
  const [percent, setPercent] = useState<number | null>(null);

  async function handleChange(
    e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>,
  ): Promise<void> {
    const file = e.target.files?.[0];
    if (!file) return;

    setPercent(0);
    await axios.postForm("/api/avatar", { avatar: file }, {
      onUploadProgress: (event: AxiosProgressEvent) => {
        setPercent(Math.round((event.progress ?? 0) * 100));
      },
    });
    setPercent(100);
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor="avatar">Avatar</label>
      <input id="avatar" type="file" onChange={handleChange} />
      {percent !== null && (
        <progress value={percent} m
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

**Multiplying `progress` without handling `undefined`.** The optional fields are optional for a reason, and strict TypeScript will not let you forget: Fix it with a nullish fallback, or branch on `lengthComputable` and render an indeterminate bar: **Treating `bytes` as a running total.** `bytes` is the delta since the previous event. Writing `setLoaded(e.bytes)` makes the bar jump backwards, because the last chunk of a transfer is usually smaller than the middle ones. Read `loaded` for the running total. **Expecting `onUploadProgress` on a `GET`.** A `GET` has no request body, so the callback never fires and the bar sits at zero forever. If you want feedback while data comes back, that is `onDownloadProgress`.

§06-004 Axios with TypeScript

2 Lessons 00m00s / 00m00s
Three labelled slots on a shipping form The concept Minimal example Predict the render Reference: config that shapes the request Reference: `AxiosHeaders`
Build Modern Web Apps with React, Hooks, State Management, and APIs Using Vite or Next.js Core concepts and theming with tailwind.config.js
05m23s

In-depth walkthrough of Axios with TypeScript, examining real-world production implementations, rendering performance, and TypeScript contracts.

Official Documentation References
Axios Official Documentation — Promise-based HTTP client for the browser and node.js.
Axios: Interceptors Reference — Intercepting requests and responses before handling.
📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

A courier form has three boxes you fill in: what is in the parcel, what the receipt will look like, and what you handed over at the counter. Get any of the three wrong and the paperwork still ships, but the person opening the parcel at the other end finds something they did not expect. Every axios request method has the same three boxes, and they are type parameters:

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

The typed-wrapper pattern from this chapter is the layer everything above it plugs into. TanStack Query's `queryFn` is typed by what your function returns, so `useQuery({ queryFn: () => getUser(id) })` infers `User` with no extra annotation; get the wrapper's return type wrong and every component reading that query is wrong too. React Hook Form's submit handler feeds your `CreateUserBody` type straight into `createUser`, and a mismatch between the form's field names and the body type surfaces at compile time instead of as a 422 in staging. The class of bug this prevents is the silent envelope leak: an `AxiosResponse<User>` passed around as if it were a `User`, discovered three components later when someone reads `user.name` and gets `undefined`. The `isAxiosError` guard prevents the other common one, a `catch` block that assumes `error.response.status` exists and throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'status')` the first time the network actually drops.

Key Code / CLI Example
import axios, { type AxiosInstance } from "axios";

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

const api: AxiosInstance = axios.create({
  baseURL: "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com",
});

const response = await api.get<User>("/users/1");

response.data.name; // string
response.status; // number
response.headers["content-type"]; // AxiosHeaderValue
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

Core Definition & Architectural Role

A courier form has three boxes you fill in: what is in the parcel, what the receipt will look like, and what you handed over at the counter. Get any of the three wrong and the paperwork still ships, but the person opening the parcel at the other end finds something they did not expect. Every axios request method has the same three boxes, and they are type parameters:

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

The typed-wrapper pattern from this chapter is the layer everything above it plugs into. TanStack Query's `queryFn` is typed by what your function returns, so `useQuery({ queryFn: () => getUser(id) })` infers `User` with no extra annotation; get the wrapper's return type wrong and every component reading that query is wrong too. React Hook Form's submit handler feeds your `CreateUserBody` type straight into `createUser`, and a mismatch between the form's field names and the body type surfaces at compile time instead of as a 422 in staging. The class of bug this prevents is the silent envelope leak: an `AxiosResponse<User>` passed around as if it were a `User`, discovered three components later when someone reads `user.name` and gets `undefined`. The `isAxiosError` guard prevents the other common one, a `catch` block that assumes `error.response.status` exists and throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'status')` the first time the network actually drops.

import axios, { type AxiosInstance } from "axios";

interface User {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
}

const api: AxiosInstance = axios.create({
  baseURL: "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com",
});

const response = await api.get<User>("/users/1");

response.data.name; // string
response.status; // number
response.headers["content-type"]; // AxiosHeaderValue
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

**Typing the variable instead of the generic.** These are not the same: The promise resolves to the envelope. Destructure `{ data }` or read `response.data`. **Using `any` to silence the interceptor config error.** `api.interceptors.request.use((config: any) => ...)` compiles and throws away every guarantee on the config, including that `config.headers` has a `set` method. Name `InternalAxiosRequestConfig` instead. **Assuming `T` validates the payload.** `api.get<User[]>("/users")` on an endpoint that returns `{ items: User[] }` type-checks perfectly and then `users.map` throws:

📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

Two pieces of axios sit between your code and the network. The **adapter** is the plug on the wall: `XMLHttpRequest` in a browser, Node's `http` module on a server, `fetch` when you ask for it. The **interceptor** is the mail-sorting room between your desk and the plug: every request walks through a stack of request handlers before it leaves, every response walks back through a stack of response handlers before it reaches you. The two are independent. You can swap the adapter without touching interceptors, and you can register interceptors without caring which adapter is in use. Each one solves a different problem.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Two pieces of axios sit between your code and the network. The **adapter** is the plug on the wall: `XMLHttpRequest` in a browser, Node's `http` module on a server, `fetch` when you ask for it. The **interceptor** is the mail-sorting room between your desk and the plug: every request walks through a stack of request handlers before it leaves, every response walks back through a stack of response handlers before it reaches you. The two are independent. You can swap the adapter without touching interceptors, and you can register interceptors without caring which adapter is in use. Each one solves a different problem.

Key Code / CLI Example
axios.get("/api/posts", { adapter: "fetch" });
// or a custom function:
axios.get("/api/posts", { adapter: myCustomAdapter });
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

**Returning a resolved value from a rejection handler.** Every downstream `try/await` then sees a success with `undefined` data. Always re-reject: **Storing the controller for abort in state.** Aborting is not a rendering concern. State updates on every upload start re-render for no visual reason. Use a ref: **Trusting `progress` (0..1) when `total` is unknown.** It is `undefined`. Mapping that to `0` produces a bar frozen at zero while bytes move. **Setting `Content-Type: multipart/form-data` by hand.** The browser generates the `boundary` token per request. Hand-writing the header produces a body the server cannot split, and the server replies `400` with an empty-looking body. Use `postForm` or let axios derive it.

Core Definition & Architectural Role

A web app sits behind a server that wants to make sure the form being submitted really came from a page the server itself rendered. The classic way is a "double-submit" cookie: when the server sends the page, it drops a cookie called `XSRF-TOKEN` (or similar) into the browser. When the browser later sends a POST, it must echo that token back in a request header (often `X-XSRF-TOKEN`). The attacker can trigger a request, but they cannot read the cookie value from a different origin, so they cannot forge the header. Axios already does this echo for you in the browser. The interesting question is "when." Two independent switches decide that:

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A web app sits behind a server that wants to make sure the form being submitted really came from a page the server itself rendered. The classic way is a "double-submit" cookie: when the server sends the page, it drops a cookie called `XSRF-TOKEN` (or similar) into the browser. When the browser later sends a POST, it must echo that token back in a request header (often `X-XSRF-TOKEN`). The attacker can trigger a request, but they cannot read the cookie value from a different origin, so they cannot forge the header. Axios already does this echo for you in the browser. The interesting question is "when." Two independent switches decide that:

Key Code / CLI Example
const api = axios.create({
  baseURL: "https://api.example.com",
  xsrfCookieName: "XSRF-TOKEN",
  xsrfHeaderName: "X-XSRF-TOKEN",
});
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

**Setting `withXSRFToken: true` without `withCredentials: true` on a cross-origin request.** The browser may refuse to send the cookie, in which case axios has nothing to put in the header, and the request goes out without CSRF protection. The two flags are independent; both are needed. **Hand-writing `Content-Type: multipart/form-data` on a `FormData` body.** The boundary in the header must match the one axios generates. Pre-baked headers produce a body the server cannot split. Let axios derive it. **Reading `config.headers["Authorization"]` directly.** After defaults are merged, `config.headers` is an `AxiosHeaders` instance with `get`/`set`/`has`. Direct indexing works on the default axios exports' loose header shape but fails type-check under strict mode for the internal config. **R

📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

Imagine a vending machine. You walk up, press a button (the `queryKey`), and the machine either gives you a snack (the `data`) or a red error light (the `error`). Either way, the machine also flips one of two small flags: `isFetching` (the coil is humming, a request is in flight right now) and `isPending` / `isError` / `isSuccess` (the most recent attempt settled into this state). The interesting part is the clipboard the machine keeps behind the counter. When you press the same button a second time, the machine first checks the clipboard. If the entry is fresh enough, you get the snack immediately and the coil never hums. If the entry is stale, you get the snack from the clipboard and the machine kicks off a quiet refill in the background. A second customer pressing the same button in the same instant gets the same in-flight request, not a duplicate. The clipboard is the cache; the button is the `queryKey`; the refill is background refetching; the dedup is request deduplication.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Imagine a vending machine. You walk up, press a button (the `queryKey`), and the machine either gives you a snack (the `data`) or a red error light (the `error`). Either way, the machine also flips one of two small flags: `isFetching` (the coil is humming, a request is in flight right now) and `isPending` / `isError` / `isSuccess` (the most recent attempt settled into this state). The interesting part is the clipboard the machine keeps behind the counter. When you press the same button a second time, the machine first checks the clipboard. If the entry is fresh enough, you get the snack immediately and the coil never hums. If the entry is stale, you get the snack from the clipboard and the machine kicks off a quiet refill in the background. A second customer pressing the same button in the same instant gets the same in-flight request, not a duplicate. The clipboard is the cache; the button is the `queryKey`; the refill is background refetching; the dedup is request deduplication.

Key Code / CLI Example
import { QueryClient, QueryClientProvider } from "@tanstack/react-query";

const queryClient = new QueryClient({
  defaultOptions: {
    queries: {
      staleTime: 60_000,
      retry: 1,
    },
  },
});

export function App({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      {children}
    </QueryClientProvider>
  );
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

**Treating `isPending` as the only loading flag.** A query can have cached data and still be fetching in the background. Showing a spinner whenever `isFetching` is true defeats the point of the cache. Show a spinner on `isPending`; show a "refreshing" hint on `isFetching` only when the cached data is already on screen. **Reading `id` from a closure but not putting it in `queryKey`.** The cache entry is keyed by the array, not by what the `queryFn` closes over. A `queryKey` of `["post"]` with a `queryFn` that reads `id` from props will keep returning the post for the first `id` you mounted with. **Forgetting `signal` in the `queryFn`.** A `queryFn` that calls `fetch(url)` without forwarding the signal still works, but unmount mid-request does not cancel the network call. 📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

Picture a cafeteria line with one slot where every tray comes out. The slot has no labels, so every tray looks like mystery food: that is `fetch(url).json()` returning `Promise<any>`. You can shove the tray into a plate (`as Promise<Post[]>`) and pretend, but the kitchen never actually shaped it. The pattern in this chapter is to put a small, typed hatchet in front of the slot. One wrapper module, generic in `<T>`, hands every caller a tray that already says `Post[]` or `User` on it. Errors throw, not return, so a failed fetch surfaces as a normal promise rejection that TanStack Query can retry, narrow, and render.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Picture a cafeteria line with one slot where every tray comes out. The slot has no labels, so every tray looks like mystery food: that is `fetch(url).json()` returning `Promise<any>`. You can shove the tray into a plate (`as Promise<Post[]>`) and pretend, but the kitchen never actually shaped it. The pattern in this chapter is to put a small, typed hatchet in front of the slot. One wrapper module, generic in `<T>`, hands every caller a tray that already says `Post[]` or `User` on it. Errors throw, not return, so a failed fetch surfaces as a normal promise rejection that TanStack Query can retry, narrow, and render.

Key Code / CLI Example
// src/api.ts
export class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(public readonly status: number, message: string) {
    super(message);
    this.name = "HttpError";
  }
}

export async function getJson<T>(url: string, init?: RequestInit): Promise<T> {
  const res = await fetch(url, init);
  if (!res.ok) {
    throw new HttpError(res.status, `HTTP ${res.status} on ${url}`);
  }
  return res.json() as Promise<T>;
}

export async function postJson<T, B>(url: string, body: B): Promise<T> {
  const res = await fetch(url, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  });
  if (!res.ok) {
    throw new HttpError(res.status, `HTTP ${res.status} on ${url}`);
  }
  return res.json() as Promise<T>;
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

**Reading `response.json()` without a type and threading `any` downstream.** Every consumer then re-narrows on every read. The fix is the wrapper: `getJson<T>(url)` returns `Promise<T>` and the cast lives in one place. **Returning `void` from a `queryFn` because the side effect "is the point."** TanStack Query will cache `undefined`, the linter will flag it, and `data` is wrong forever. The fix is to return the response body, even when the body is `{ ok: true }`; cache the value. **Using `enabled: true` everywhere because "the dependent query is always going to run."** When the upstream dependency fails, the downstream query still fires with `undefined` input and either crashes or returns the wrong shape. The fix is `enabled: user.isSuccess`. **Treating TanStack Query as a replacement f

**Reading `response.json()` without a type and threading `any` downstream.** Every consumer then re-narrows on every read. The fix is the wrapper: `getJson<T>(url)` returns `Promise<T>` and the cast lives in one place. **Returning `void` from a `queryFn` because the side effect "is the point."** TanStack Query will cache `undefined`, the linter will flag it, and `data` is wrong forever. The fix is to return the response body, even when the body is `{ ok: true }`; cache the value. **Using `enabled: true` everywhere because "the dependent query is always going to run."** When the upstream dependency fails, the downstream query still fires with `undefined` input and either crashes or returns the wrong shape. The fix is `enabled: user.isSuccess`. **Treating TanStack Query as a replacement f

Core Definition & Architectural Role

The previous chapter ended with the read side: `useQuery`, `queryKey`, the cache, the `isPending` / `isSuccess` / `isFetching` flags. This chapter is the write side. Imagine the same vending-machine clipboard. A successful mutation (a POST, a PATCH, a DELETE) changes what the server has, so every cache entry that depends on it is now stale. The mutation does not know which entries are affected; the cache does. The bridge between them is `queryClient.invalidateQueries(...)`. `invalidateQueries` does two things: it marks matching entries stale, and (for active entries) it triggers a refetch. An inactive entry is just marked stale and waits; an active entry is marked stale and refetched immediately. Returning or awaiting the resulting Promise keeps the mutation pending until any refetches settle.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

**Forgetting to invalidate after a mutation.** The mutation's response is the truth for *one* record; every list, every aggregate, every dependent view is still showing the pre-mutation snapshot. The fix is `onSuccess` / `onSettled` calling `invalidateQueries` on every affected `queryKey`. **Invalidating a `queryKey` that does not match.** `["posts"]` matches `["posts"]` and any `["posts", ...]` prefix, but it does not match `["post", 1]`. A typo (`"post"` singular vs `"posts"` plural) silently leaves the cache stale. The fix is to keep the `queryKey` literal in one place, typically an exported `queryKeys` object, so invalidation calls cannot drift from the keys the queries actually use. **Awaiting `invalidateQueries` and then assuming every entry refetched.** Awaiting the returned Promi

Core Definition & Architectural Role

A newsroom has reporters, editors, and a wall of clipboards. Reporters phone in stories; editors update the clipboards so the print room can pull the latest version of any headline. The wall is the **server state**: data that lives somewhere else, changes on its own schedule, and needs to be shared across every desk. Before TanStack Query, the React app's "wall" was a patchwork of `useState` per component, a `useEffect` per fetch, a `refreshKey` counter, and a ref to keep the count of "have we fetched this yet?" Each component kept its own clipboard. The same URL got hit twice from two siblings. A component unmounting in the middle of a fetch leaked the request. A new component mounting right after refetched the same data it would have got in five seconds anyway.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A newsroom has reporters, editors, and a wall of clipboards. Reporters phone in stories; editors update the clipboards so the print room can pull the latest version of any headline. The wall is the **server state**: data that lives somewhere else, changes on its own schedule, and needs to be shared across every desk. Before TanStack Query, the React app's "wall" was a patchwork of `useState` per component, a `useEffect` per fetch, a `refreshKey` counter, and a ref to keep the count of "have we fetched this yet?" Each component kept its own clipboard. The same URL got hit twice from two siblings. A component unmounting in the middle of a fetch leaked the request. A new component mounting right after refetched the same data it would have got in five seconds anyway.

Key Code / CLI Example
function PostList(): React.ReactElement {
  const [filter, setFilter] = useState("");           // client state
  const { data, isPending } = useQuery({              // server state
    queryKey: ["posts", filter],
    queryFn: () => fetchPosts(filter),
  });
  ...
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

- **Forgetting the provider.** Calling `useQuery` outside a `QueryClientProvider` throws `No QueryClient set`. The fix is a single provider at the root, not per-page providers. - **`new QueryClient()` inside a component.** The cache is reset on every render. The client must live at module scope (or in a `useState` factory if you need tests to construct fresh ones). - **Mutation result rest-destructuring.** `const { mutate, ...rest } = useMutation(...)` subscribes the component to every tracked property. Pull only the fields the render reads. - **Not forwarding the `signal` in `queryFn`.** The query keeps running after unmount; the response lands in a cache entry no observer is rendering. Always `fetch(url, { signal })` or `api.get(url, { signal })`. - **Invalidating the wrong prefix.** `in

Core Definition & Architectural Role

Difficulty: 1-2 · Prerequisites: Server State with TanStack Query, MUI Timeline component A mutation is a write to the server. The write may be a `POST`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE`, and it may leave several cached reads out of date. This chapter focuses on the two handles that `useMutation` gives you for starting that write, then connects that choice to callbacks, invalidation, query keys, and application-wide pending indicators.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

A form submit often needs only `mutate`: the button can show `isPending`, and `onSuccess` can invalidate the affected list. A wizard or a “save then navigate” action needs `mutateAsync`, because the next step depends on the returned record. A shared `mutationOptions` function keeps those choices consistent across buttons, global `useIsMutating` indicators, and cache-level calls. The same distinction appears in an activity feed or an MUI `Timeline`. A saved event changes the timeline list, a detail view, and perhaps a summary count. Correct query keys tell invalidation which entries to refresh. Correct query-function returns give those entries real cache data. Network state and `fetchStatus` let the timeline explain why it is waiting instead of showing a spinner with no context.

Key Code / CLI Example
import { useMutation } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import type { ReactElement } from "react";

type Todo = { id: number; title: string };
type NewTodo = { title: string };

async function createTodo(input: NewTodo): Promise<Todo> {
  const response = await fetch("/api/todos", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(input),
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return (await response.json()) as Todo;
}

export function AddTodoButton(): ReactElement {
  const { mutate, isPending, isError, error } = useMutation({
    mutationFn: createTodo,
  });

  return (
    <section>
      <button
        type="button"
        disabled={isPending}
        onClick={() => mutate({ title: "Read the cache" })}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

The following snippet is deliberately broken: Use `mutation.mutateAsync(...)` for the assignment, or keep `mutate(...)` and move follow-up work into `onSuccess`. The following snippet is deliberately broken: Return the response body. At runtime, a query that resolves to `undefined` cannot provide cache data and TanStack Query reports that query data is undefined.

Core Definition & Architectural Role

Difficulty: 2 · Prerequisites: `mutate` (`void`) vs `mutateAsync` (`Promise`) function signatures, Queries and query result states, Generic fetch wrapper module, MUI Timeline component, Server State with TanStack Query A query is `pending` on its very first render. That is the right behaviour for a brand-new cache entry, but it produces two visual problems the user can feel:

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

`placeholderData` is the option that turns TanStack Query from a cache into a UI primitive. A list with `placeholderData: keepPreviousData` reads as "the previous page, then the new page, without a spinner"; a detail with a `placeholderData` function reads as "the preview from the list, then the full post, without a spinner." The patterns show up in every real-world app that has a paginated list, a list-with-detail, or any screen whose data lives in a different cache entry than the screen the user is currently on. The same chapter covers the supporting machinery (`isPlaceholderData`, query functions, cache lifecycle, retries, prefetching, polling, invalidation, mutation callbacks) because each one shows up alongside `placeholderData` in a production codebase.

Key Code / CLI Example
import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import type { ReactElement } from "react";

interface Todo { readonly id: number; readonly title: string; }
const placeholderTodos: ReadonlyArray<Todo> = [
  { id: 0, title: "Loading…" },
];

export function Todos(): ReactElement {
  const { data, isPlaceholderData } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ["todos"] as const,
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => fetch("/api/todos", { signal }).then((r) => r.json() as Promise<Todo[]>),
    placeholderData: placeholderTodos,
  });

  return (
    <ul style={{ opacity: isPlaceholderData ? 0.6 : 1 }}>
      {data.map((t) => <li key={t.id}>{t.title}</li>)}
    </ul>
  );
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

- **Confusing `placeholderData` with `initialData`.** Both make the query start in `success`, but only `initialData` is written to the cache. A `placeholderData` value is dropped the moment the real `queryFn` resolves; an `initialData` value lives in the cache until `staleTime` expires. - **Forgetting to gate the "Next" button on `isPlaceholderData`.** Without the gate, the user can click twice for one fetch and the page index advances by two. The flag exists exactly for this. - **Returning `undefined` from a function-form `placeholderData`.** That is the "no placeholder" signal. The query falls back to `pending`. Use it deliberately, not by accident. - **Forwarding `placeholderData` to a value that comes from the same key.** `placeholderData` is rendered before the `queryFn` resolves. If

Core Definition & Architectural Role

Difficulty: 2 · Prerequisites: `mutate` (`void`) vs `mutateAsync` (`Promise`) function signatures, Placeholder query data, Server State with TanStack Query, MUI Timeline component, Generic fetch wrapper module A `useQuery` call duplicates the same three arguments across the component that reads the data, the route loader that prefetches it, the SSR dehydration that ships it to the client, and the devtools entry that inspects it: the `queryKey`, the `queryFn`, and a handful of per-query options (`staleTime`, `retry`, `select`). If any of those drift, the cache treats the entries as different and the app silently fetches twice.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

The `queryOptions` helper is the seam between "the cache contract for this resource" and "every consumer that reads or writes that cache." Without it, the contract lives in five places (a hook, a prefetch, three call sites that invalidate) and drift is inevitable. With it, the contract lives in one file and every consumer gets typed access for free. The pattern shows up in real codebases in three places:

Key Code / CLI Example
import { queryOptions } from "@tanstack/react-query";

interface Post {
  readonly id: number;
  readonly title: string;
}

async function fetchPost(id: number, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<Post> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/posts/${id}`, { signal });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  return res.json() as Promise<Post>;
}

export function postQueryOptions(id: number) {
  return queryOptions({
    queryKey: ["post", id] as const,
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => fetchPost(id, signal),
    staleTime: 60_000,
  });
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

- **Forgetting `as const` on the `queryKey`.** Without it, the `queryKey` type widens to `string[]` and the brand on `queryOptions` is weaker. Most editors will still infer the right shape, but the brand's `TData` resolution goes through `unknown[]` and the type goes fuzzy at `getQueryData` call sites. - **Re-defining the options at each call site.** The single biggest reason `queryOptions` exists is to remove duplication. If a component hand-writes `{ queryKey: ["post", id], queryFn: ({ signal }) => fetchPost(id, signal) }` next to `useQuery`, the helper is not paying its rent. - **Calling `getQueryData` with a raw key and a generic.** `queryClient.getQueryData<Post>(["post", 1])` is what you do when there is no helper. Once the helper exists, `getQueryData(postQueryOptions(1))` is the ty

Core Definition & Architectural Role

Difficulty: 2 to 3 · Prerequisites: `mutate` (`void`) vs `mutateAsync` (`Promise`) function signatures, `queryOptions`, Server State with TanStack Query, MUI Timeline component A `<NetworkIndicator>` is the small global affordance that says "your app is talking to the server." It usually sits in a top app bar, and it is supposed to reflect *every* in-flight query, not only the one a particular component knows about. There is a TanStack Query hook for exactly that job: `useIsFetching` returns the count of queries currently in `fetching` state, optionally filtered by `queryKey` prefix, `predicate`, or `queryClient`. It subscribes once, like `useQuery`, and updates in real time as queries start and stop.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

The advanced API surface is where TanStack Query differentiates from a hand-rolled `useEffect` + `fetch`. Five patterns show up in real codebases: - **Global status indicators.** A `<NetworkIndicator>` driven by `useIsFetching`, paired with a `<MutationIndicator>` driven by `useIsMutationStatus`. The pattern is one component per global concern. - **Dashboards with N parallel entries.** `useQueries` (with `combine`) is the canonical shape for a dashboard. Each tile gets a row in the result array, and the consumer flattens or aggregates as needed. - **Infinite feeds.** `useInfiniteQuery` is the right hook for chat histories, search results, comment threads. The "Load more" pattern is one `fetchNextPage` button per page boundary. - **Dependent data.** A user → team, an order → customer, a project → members tree. `enabled` (or `skipToken`) expresses the waterfall explicitly and keeps TypeScript narrowing clean. - **SSR data transfer.** `dehydrate` on the server, `<HydrationBoundary>` on the client. The pattern removes the "Loading…" flash for every page that ships prefetched data.

Key Code / CLI Example
import { useIsFetching } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import type { ReactElement } from "react";

export function NetworkIndicator(): ReactElement {
  const isFetching = useIsFetching();
  return (
    <div aria-live="polite" aria-busy={isFetching > 0}>
      {isFetching > 0 ? `Loading ${isFetching}…` : "Idle"}
    </div>
  );
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

- **Treating `useIsFetching` as a per-query hook.** It is a global subscriber. Reading it on a screen with no queries returns `0`; reading it on a screen with N queries returns N if every query is fetching in parallel. Use it for a global indicator, not a per-row spinner. - **Forgetting `enabled` on a dependent query.** A second query that reads `user.data?.teamId` without an `enabled` flag will fetch with `teamId: undefined` on first render, fail, and only fix itself after the user query resolves. The pattern is `enabled: user.data !== undefined` or `queryFn: user.data ? fetchTeam(user.data.teamId, signal) : skipToken`. - **Reading `data` outside the `isSuccess` branch.** `queryFn` may not have resolved yet. The pattern is `if (isPending) return <Loading/>; if (isError) return <Error/>; r

Core Definition & Architectural Role

Difficulty: 1 to 3 · Prerequisites: Server State with TanStack Query, `queryOptions`, `mutate` (`void`) vs `mutateAsync` (`Promise`) function signatures, Placeholder query data, Queries and query result states, MUI Timeline component, `useActionState` + React 19 Form Actions, Generic fetch wrapper module, JSX and Rendering A mobile dashboard boots up. The device is on the train, the LTE drops in and out, the user pulls to refresh, and TanStack Query has to decide, for every entry in the cache, whether to fire the request, sit in `paused`, or go to `error` right now. The setting that drives the answer is `networkMode`, and the default is the one that almost fits: `online`. Three modes ship (`online`, `always`, `offlineFirst`), and the right pick depends on whether the underlying data source is the network, a local store, or a service-worker cache.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

The advanced surface is where TanStack Query differentiates from a hand-rolled `useEffect` + `fetch`. Five patterns show up in real codebases: - **Connectivity-aware dashboards.** `networkMode: 'online'` + an offline banner that checks `isPaused`. The user sees the right affordance instead of a spinner. - **Local-only stores.** `networkMode: 'always'` for `AsyncStorage` reads, paired with a `Promise.resolve(value)` `queryFn`. The same hook surface, no network dependency. - **Service-worker PWA.** `networkMode: 'offlineFirst'` for cache-backed entries. The first fetch comes from cache; the retry is paused if the cache misses. - **Dashboards with N parallel entries.** `useQueries` (with `combine`) is the canonical shape. Each tile gets a row in the result array, and the consumer flattens or aggregates. - **Search-as-you-type.** `prefetchQuery` on hover, `cancelQueries` on each new keystroke, `useInfiniteQuery` for the result list. The cache, the network, and the UI all coordinate through the same primitives.

Key Code / CLI Example
new QueryClient({
  defaultOptions: {
    queries: { networkMode: "always" },
    mutations: { networkMode: "always" },
  },
});
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

- **Showing a loading spinner on a paused query.** A `networkMode: 'online'` query that mounts while offline reads `isPending: true` and `isPaused: true`. The right UI is "you're offline" with a retry, not an infinite spinner. - **Setting `networkMode: 'always'` to "fix" a paused query.** The mode is for non-network data sources. Use the wrong one and a real connectivity loss no longer pauses; it retries, fails, and burns battery. - **Forgetting `enabled` on a dependent query.** A second query that reads `user.data?.teamId` without an `enabled` flag fires with `teamId: undefined` on first render, fails, and only fixes itself after the user query resolves. The pattern is `enabled: user.data !== undefined` or `queryFn: user.data ? fetchTeam(user.data.teamId, signal) : skipToken`. - **Rest-sp

Core Definition & Architectural Role

Difficulty: 2 to 3 · Prerequisites: `mutate` (`void`) vs `mutateAsync` (`Promise`) function signatures, Network mode (online / always / offlineFirst), Server State with TanStack Query, Queries and query result states, `queryOptions`, `useIsFetching` A React Server Component renders a project list. The server already fetched every row, so when the client hydrates, the first paint shows the data with no spinner. A second screen is a settings page that opens to a search box; the user has not typed yet, but the page must not fire a request for `""`. A third screen is an offline PWA: the user closes the laptop, opens it on the train a day later, and the dashboard still shows yesterday's numbers before the network reconnects. A fourth surface streams progress from a long-running job.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

The advanced surface is where TanStack Query differentiates from a hand-rolled `useEffect` + `fetch`. Five patterns show up in real codebases: - **Conditional fetches.** `skipToken` is the canonical "do not fire until a value is ready" pattern. Search boxes, dependent queries, lazy detail panels all use it. - **SSR handoff.** A server that prefetches and a client that hydrates from `dehydrate` give the user the first paint with no spinner. The consumer code is identical to CSR; the boundary is the only difference. - **Offline-first PWAs.** `persistQueryClient` with a sync or async persister keeps the cache alive across reloads. `IsRestoringProvider` makes the restore race-free. - **Streaming jobs.** `streamedQuery` is the canonical "tokens arrive over time" pattern. The reducer form folds chunks into a single derived value as they arrive. - **Suspense integration.** `useSuspenseQuery` removes the `isPending` branch from the consumer and routes errors to error boundaries. The trade-off is real boundaries and no `enabled`.

Key Code / CLI Example
import { skipToken, useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import type { ReactElement } from "react";

interface User { readonly id: number; readonly name: string; }

async function fetchUser(id: number, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<User> {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${id}`, { signal });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  return (await res.json()) as User;
}

export function UserPanel({ userId }: { userId: number | null }): ReactElement {
  const { data, isPending } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ["user", userId] as const,
    queryFn: userId === null
      ? skipToken
      : ({ signal }) => fetchUser(userId, signal),
  });

  if (userId === null) return <p>Pick a user</p>;
  if (isPending) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  return <p>{data!.name}</p>;
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

- **Passing `enabled: false` and a real `queryFn`.** The hook type-checks, but the `queryFn` is dead code on every render and the consumer can still call `refetch`. Use `skipToken` when the disable is permanent; use `enabled: false` when a `refetch` may run later. - **Confusing `skipToken` with `null`.** `null` is not assignable to `queryFn`; the type checker rejects it. `skipToken` is the only sentinel the overload set accepts. - **Forgetting `<HydrationBoundary>` on the client.** A server that dehydrates and a client that mounts `useQuery` without the boundary fires the network request anyway. The boundary is the merge step. - **Restoring the cache outside `<IsRestoringProvider>`.** Consumers mount before the merge runs; the first render reads empty and fires the `queryFn`. The flag is w

Core Definition & Architectural Role

Difficulty: 2 to 3 · Prerequisites: Server State with TanStack Query, `queryOptions`, Invalidating queries after mutations, `mutate` and `mutateAsync` Think of the in-memory query cache as a desk and Web Storage as a locker. The desk is fast, but a page reload clears it. A persister periodically puts a labeled snapshot in the locker. On the next visit, TanStack Query can return the snapshot to the desk before components start new requests.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Persistence improves reload and offline startup behavior, but it adds a second cache lifetime. `gcTime`, `maxAge`, `buster`, storage quota, query-key design, and mutation updates now affect whether the UI shows current data. The broader API map helps you choose one operation with the right contract. It prevents duplicate fetches from using `fetchQuery` where `ensureQueryData` fits, stale responses from overwriting optimistic updates, and list/detail cache entries from drifting after a mutation. The type helpers catch key and data mismatches before those paths reach a browser.

Core Definition & Architectural Role

Difficulty: 2–4 · Prerequisites: Synchronous storage persister, Server State with TanStack Query, Queries and query result states, `skipToken` Imagine a library with two storage systems. The reading room holds every book currently in use. An archive holds books between visits. You could copy the entire reading room into the archive whenever one book changes, or file each book under its own catalogue number and retrieve it only when someone asks for it.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Persistence makes repeat visits fast and supports offline-first screens, but stale private data and mismatched cache keys are harder to notice than a failed request. A clear policy for identity, freshness, storage expiry, and restoration prevents cross-user data leaks and surprise refetches. Concurrent prefetching also removes latency that nested component fetches add one request at a time.

Key Code / CLI Example
import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import { experimental_createQueryPersister } from "@tanstack/react-query-persist-client";

interface Settings {
  readonly theme: "light" | "dark";
}

const settingsPersister = experimental_createQueryPersister({
  storage: window.localStorage,
  maxAge: 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  prefix: "course",
});

async function getSettings(): Promise<Settings> {
  const response = await fetch("/api/settings");
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json() as Promise<Settings>;
}

export function SettingsPanel() {
  const query = useQuery({
    queryKey: ["settings"] as const,
    queryFn: getSettings,
    staleTime: 5 * 60 * 1000,
    persister: settingsPersister.persisterFn,
  });

  if (query.isPending) return
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

`@tanstack/eslint-plugin-query` supplies recommended rules for React Query code. Its exhaustive-key rule reports a query function variable that is absent from `queryKey`. The stable-client rule catches a `QueryClient` recreated during each render. Other rules cover unstable dependencies, infinite-query property order, and mutation callback usage. If the function requests `/api/projects?owner=${owner}`, then `owner` belongs in `queryKey`: The key is both a cache address and a dependency list. Leaving `owner` out can show one user's cached projects after the prop changes.

📝Comprehensive Study Notes & Mental ModelQuick Review
Expand NotesCollapse
Core Definition & Architectural Role

Difficulty: 2 to 3 · Prerequisites: Server State with TanStack Query, `placeholderData`, `queryOptions`, Per-query experimental persister, Generic fetch wrapper module, `useActionState` + React 19 Form Actions, `useIsFetching`, `mutate` (`void`) vs `mutateAsync` (`Promise`) function signatures, Network mode (online / always / offlineFirst), `useContext` A search box renders before the user types. The shape of the request depends on the value in the box, and the value is `""` on first paint. A detail panel sits in a sidebar that opens to a row the user has not clicked yet. A dropdown lets the user pick a project from a list, and the dependent request ("show me the members of project X") cannot fire until the user picks something. None of these should hit the network, and none of them should throw a TypeScript error because the function signature demands a value that does not exist yet.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

The class of bug `skipToken` solves is "the query fires before the input is ready and the consumer lies". Search boxes, dependent dropdowns, lazy detail panels, and edit screens all hit this. The runtime version (`enabled: false`) loads the lying into the consumer: the consumer has to remember to early-return on a missing value, has to remember not to call `refetch`, and the `data` type is wrong (`User | undefined` even when the hook is permanently disabled). The `skipToken` version makes the type system enforce the contract. The factory pattern (`queryOptions` + `skipToken`) is the cleanest way to write a single piece of logic that handles both "fetch" and "do not fetch yet". The shared state that drives the toggle lives in the narrowest scope that fits the consumer (state, URL, context, cache). The `queryFn` forwards `signal` so unmount and re-render cancel in-flight work. The cache is one per module, the invalidation is the narrowest key, and the `eslint-plugin-query` rules catch the property-order traps before they reach a reviewer.

Key Code / CLI Example
import { skipToken, useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import type { ReactElement } from "react";

interface User { readonly id: number; readonly name: string; }

function fetchUser(id: number, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<User> {
  return fetch(`/api/users/${id}`, { signal }).then((r) => {
    if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${r.status}`);
    return r.json() as Promise<User>;
  });
}

export function UserPanel({ userId }: { userId: number | null }): ReactElement {
  const { data, isPending } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ["user", userId] as const,
    queryFn: userId === null ? skipToken : ({ signal }) => fetchUser(userId, signal),
  });

  if (userId === null) return <p>Pick a user</p>;
  if (isPending) return <p>Loading…</p>;
  return <p>{data!.name}</p>;
}
⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

- **Using `enabled: false` and a real `queryFn` when the disable is permanent.** The hook type-checks, the `queryFn` is dead code, and the consumer can still call `refetch`. Use `skipToken` for the permanent case. - **Confusing `skipToken` with `null` or `undefined`.** Neither is assignable to `queryFn`. `skipToken` is the only sentinel the overload set accepts. - **Forgetting to wrap dependent queries in `skipToken`.** A query that depends on a `null` upstream value fires `undefined` and 404s. The factory pattern (`membersQueryOptions(project.data ? { projectId } : null)`) is the fix. - **Wrapping a `useQuery` that does an `await` in a `useEffect` without forwarding `signal`.** The `queryFn` receives `signal` already; forward it to `fetch`. Otherwise the unmount does not cancel the in-fli

Core Definition & Architectural Role

Difficulty: 2 to 4 · Prerequisites: `skipToken` and `UnusedSkipTokenOptions`, Server State with TanStack Query, Queries and query result states, `mutate` (`void`) vs `mutateAsync` (`Promise`) function signatures, MUI Timeline component, `useReducer` with Discriminated Unions, Generic fetch wrapper module, Type-safe query disabling with `skipToken`, React Major Version Policy A typical React app has more than one way to talk to a server. TanStack Query owns the read cache and the mutation lifecycle. Redux Toolkit owns the imperative store, and `createAsyncThunk` is its bridge to async work. Apollo Client owns a normalized GraphQL cache. The framework-specific adapters (`Preact <HydrationBoundary>`, `useIsRestoring`) are ports of the React surface for non-React hosts. Each layer exists because the problem shape it solves is genuinely different, and the bug-prevention story for each is a separate lesson.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Most production React apps reach a point where they need more than one data layer. A typical app uses TanStack Query for REST reads, Redux Toolkit (with `createAsyncThunk`) for imperative flows that need global state (auth, audit logs), and Apollo Client for any GraphQL surface. Each library earns its place by solving a specific shape of problem: cache-key reads, imperative async actions, and normalized GraphQL responses, respectively. The patterns in this chapter show up in every modern React codebase that talks to a server. `createAsyncThunk` is the Redux Toolkit idiom for "fire and forget" async work that touches a slice. `useInfiniteQuery` is the canonical shape for cursor-paginated lists. Apollo's `useQuery` + `InMemoryCache` is the canonical shape for GraphQL. The patterns port across frameworks: the Preact `<HydrationBoundary>` and `useIsRestoring` mirror the React versions, and the Svelte adapter exposes the same hook surface with runes.

  Post,                 // TReturn: the resolved value
  CreatePostInput,      // TArg: the argument
  { rejectValue: RejectedPayload } // TThunkApi: config including rejectValue type
>(
  "posts/create",
  async (input, { rejectWithValue }) => {
    const res = await fetch("/api/posts", {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify(input),
    });
    if (!res.ok) return rejectWithValue({ message: `HTTP ${res.status}` });
    return (

The fix is `initialPageParam: null as string | null` (or whatever cursor type the server expects). - **Placing `getNextPageParam` before `queryFn`.** TypeScript needs the `queryFn` to infer the page type. The ESLint rule from `@tanstack/eslint-plugin-query` rejects the order. Move `queryFn` first. - **Rest-destructuring the `useInfiniteQuery` result.** `const { data, ...rest } = useInfiniteQuery(...)` subscribes to every tracked property. Pull only the fields the render reads. - **`maxPages: 1`.** Bidirectional navigation breaks once the eviction kicks in. Pick `maxPages: 5` (or higher) and define both `getNextPageParam` and

Core Definition & Architectural Role

Difficulty: 3 to 4 · Prerequisites: Server State with TanStack Query, `queryOptions`, Queries and query result states, Invalidating queries after mutations, createAsyncThunk for side effects A moving company packs your kitchen into labeled boxes, drives them across town, and unpacks them in the new kitchen. Nothing is cooked twice. The plates that existed before the move exist after it.

🧠Under-The-Hood Mental Model

Hydration is the difference between a page that shows content on the first paint and one that shows three spinners. It shows up in every framework integration you will read: Next.js App Router templates ship `providers.tsx` plus `<HydrationBoundary>`, TanStack Start does the same through its router, and Remix templates dehydrate from the `loader`. The bugs it prevents are concrete. A module-scope `QueryClient` on a server leaks one user's data into another user's page. A mismatched query key between prefetch and component quietly does nothing, so the page looks fine in development and double-fetches in production. Default `staleTime` doubles the request count on every server-rendered page. A `useSuspenseQuery` stack turns three parallel requests into three serial ones, which nobody notices on localhost and everybody notices on mobile.

Key Code / CLI Example
// pages/posts.tsx
import {
  HydrationBoundary,
  QueryClient,
  dehydrate,
  queryOptions,
  useQuery,
} from "@tanstack/react-query";
import type { DehydratedState } from "@tanstack/react-query";
import type { ReactElement } from "react";

export interface Post {
  readonly id: number;
  readonly title: string;
}

async function getPosts(): Promise<ReadonlyArray<Post>> {
  const response = await fetch("https://example.test/api/posts");
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Posts request failed: ${response.status}`);
  return (await response.json()) as ReadonlyArray<Post>;
}

export const postsQueryOptions = () =>
  queryOptions({
    queryKey: ["posts"] as const,
    queryFn: getPosts,
  });

⚠️Common Pitfall & Production Gotcha

Direct DOM mutation or impure side effects during the render phase cause hydration mismatches, duplicate executions in Strict Mode, and stale closures. Always declare full dependency arrays in useEffect and never read state during render from outside the component tree.
